questions.explanation: Batch systems take a large bounded input, run offline on a schedule, and produce output nobody is waiting on interactively. An online service is request/response and latency-critical; stream processing consumes unbounded input in near-real-time; OLTP is for transactional reads/writes, not analytic recomputation.
options: An online service — it serves user requests with low latency
A batch processing system — it processes a large bounded input offline on a schedule
A stream processing system — it consumes unbounded input in near-real-time
An OLTP database handling transactional reads and writes
questions.question: Your team runs a job every night that recomputes product recommendations from the day's clickstream; nobody waits for it and it takes hours. Which kind of system is this?

questions.explanation: The Unix philosophy is small tools composed over a uniform interface — text streams through pipes. Sorting by key colocates equal keys so a simple sequential scan can aggregate them; MapReduce's shuffle/sort is this idea distributed. Sort doesn't index, compress, or parallelize anything.
options: It builds an index so later tools can random-access the log
It compresses the log to reduce I/O between pipeline stages
It groups records with equal keys together so a sequential scan can aggregate them — the same idea behind MapReduce's shuffle/sort
It parallelizes the pipeline across multiple machines
questions.question: In the chapter's Unix log-analysis example, several small tools are chained with pipes and `sort` does the heavy lifting. What is `sort` actually accomplishing?

questions.explanation: Mappers emit key-value pairs; the framework partitions them by key, then the shuffle/sort phase delivers every key's records to one reducer, which aggregates per key. Any other order breaks the contract that a reducer sees all values for its keys.
options: Map, then partition by key, then shuffle/sort, then reduce
Reduce, then shuffle, then map
Shuffle, then map, then reduce, then partition
Map, then reduce, then shuffle, then partition
questions.question: What is the order of phases in a MapReduce job?

questions.explanation: Deterministic, side-effect-free functions mean re-running a task on the same input yields the same output, so the framework can simply retry elsewhere. HDFS replication protects stored data, not in-flight task semantics, and MapReduce uses neither two-phase commit nor a write-ahead log for tasks.
options: HDFS replication means the task's partial output is already backed up elsewhere
Hadoop coordinates tasks with two-phase commit, so the crash is rolled back cleanly
The job tracker replays the task's write-ahead log to restore its state
Map and reduce functions are deterministic and side-effect-free, so re-execution on the same input produces the same output
questions.question: A mapper task crashes halfway through a Hadoop job. Why is it safe to simply re-run it on another machine?

questions.explanation: A broadcast (map-side) hash join loads the 50 MB table into each mapper's memory and joins during the map phase — the 10 TB input is never shuffled. A reduce-side join would work but pointlessly shuffles terabytes; partitioned hash join requires both inputs pre-partitioned identically.
options: Reduce-side sort-merge join: shuffle both datasets so matching keys meet at reducers
Broadcast hash join: load the small table into memory in every mapper and join during the map phase
Partitioned hash join: join locally without shuffling either input
Nested-loop join inside the reducer
questions.question: Each night you join a 10 TB click log with a 50 MB user-profile table. Both are plain files. What is the most efficient join strategy?

questions.explanation: The book frames Hadoop as a general-purpose distributed batch platform — a 'distributed OS' for data — happy with raw schema-on-read files, versus MPP databases purpose-built for fast SQL over curated schema-on-write tables. Neither replaced the other; the ecosystems converged instead.
options: They are interchangeable; Hadoop is simply the cheaper option
MPP databases are always faster because they run on better hardware
Hadoop is a general-purpose distributed batch platform that tolerates raw, messy, schema-on-read data, while MPP databases are specialized engines for SQL analytics over clean, schema-on-write data
Hadoop made MPP databases obsolete for all analytic workloads
questions.question: Which statement best captures the book's comparison of Hadoop and MPP analytic databases?

questions.explanation: BSP means every vertex computes on local state in parallel, sends messages, then blocks at a barrier until all vertices finish — that is one superstep. Fault tolerance comes from periodic checkpointing, not deleting state, and no single vertex ever processes the whole graph.
options: A single vertex processes the entire graph
All vertices compute in parallel on their local state, send messages to other vertices, then wait at a barrier until every vertex finishes before the next superstep
The graph is re-partitioned across machines to rebalance load
Checkpoints are deleted to free up disk space
questions.question: In Pregel's bulk-synchronous-parallel model, what happens in one superstep?

questions.explanation: Reduce-side joins rely on the shuffle to colocate equal keys, and they impose no requirements on input layout — but every record crosses the network, and a hot key funnels disproportionate work onto one reducer, which is the classic skew problem.
options: The shuffle/sort phase delivers all records sharing a key to the same reducer, which can then combine them
The join logic runs inside the mapper, so no data crosses the network
They work for arbitrary join conditions without requiring the inputs to be pre-partitioned
Heavily skewed keys are handled gracefully, with load spread evenly across reducers
questions.question: Which statements about reduce-side joins are true?

questions.explanation: Workflows chain jobs as DAGs, and derived data is refreshed by deterministic recomputation, not in-place patching. MapReduce itself is low-level — multi-stage work needs chained jobs with files between them. And the partitioning terms are opposites: document-partitioned splits by document, term-partitioned by term.
options: A batch workflow is a DAG of jobs where each job's output becomes the next job's input
Derived datasets such as search indexes are kept fresh by periodically recomputing them deterministically from the inputs
In a document-partitioned index, each partition stores the postings for a subset of terms
MapReduce's model is low-level key-value callbacks, so multi-stage analytics must chain several jobs with materialized files between them
questions.question: Which statements about batch workflows are true?

questions.explanation: Hadoop's bets were data locality, commodity hardware, and re-execution-based fault tolerance, with schema applied on read — the opposite of enforcing schemas on write. Over time MPP systems absorbed Hadoop techniques and Hadoop absorbed SQL, converging the two worlds.
options: Hadoop moves compute to the data for locality rather than dragging large datasets to the computation
Hadoop assumes commodity hardware and achieves fault tolerance by re-executing deterministic tasks
Hadoop validates and enforces a schema when data is written, like a traditional MPP database
MPP databases adopted Hadoop-era techniques such as columnar storage, while Hadoop gained SQL engines like Hive, Impala, and Presto — the two converged
questions.question: Which statements about Hadoop's design and its comparison with MPP databases are true?

questions.explanation: Materializing map output to the distributed filesystem is what makes task re-execution trivially safe, but each stage pays full disk I/O plus replication. Dataflow engines trade some of that durability for speed via pipelining and in-memory intermediates — the benefit is real, so 'pure overhead' is wrong.
options: Classic MapReduce writes every map output to the distributed filesystem before the reduce phase begins
Modern dataflow engines (Spark, Tez, Flink) avoid that cost by pipelining operators or keeping intermediate state in memory
That materialization is pure overhead with no benefit, which is why no current engine does it
Writing intermediates to durable storage buys fault tolerance — a failed task's input can be re-read — at the cost of disk I/O and replication per stage
questions.question: Which statements about materialization of intermediate state are true?

questions.explanation: The chapter's arc is Unix pipes → MapReduce → dataflow engines, with partitioning/sorting/shuffle surviving every transition, and declarative layers (Pig, Hive, Spark) moving optimization into the framework. Those ideas weren't made obsolete — they were absorbed.
options: Batch processing's lineage runs from Unix pipes through MapReduce to modern dataflow engines
High-level APIs (Pig, Hive, Spark SQL/DataFrames) compile declarative queries into dataflow DAGs, letting an optimizer choose join strategies and plans
Declarative APIs made partitioning, sorting, and shuffling obsolete — modern engines no longer use them
Partitioning, sorting, and shuffle-based grouping and joins are the durable MapReduce ideas reused by every later engine

summary.overview: This chapter traces batch processing from Unix command-line pipelines through MapReduce to modern dataflow engines. Its core argument: batch systems process large bounded inputs offline on a schedule, and the durable ideas underneath them — partitioning data, sorting to group by key, and shuffling related records together — keep reappearing in every generation of tooling. Understanding these ideas, and their costs (especially around materializing intermediate state), is what lets you pick the right tool and use it well in interviews and in practice.

sections.heading: Batch Processing with Unix Tools
takeaways: Batch systems process large bounded inputs offline on a schedule (minutes to days) with no user waiting — unlike online services, which are request/response and latency-critical, and stream processing, which handles unbounded input in near-real-time.

The Unix philosophy — small, composable tools communicating over a uniform interface (text streams through pipes) — is the direct ancestor of batch frameworks; the chapter's log-analysis example chains simple tools into a pipeline.

Sorting is the fundamental grouping primitive: sorting records by key brings equal keys together so a sequential scan can aggregate them — the same trick MapReduce's shuffle/sort phase later distributed across machines.

sections.heading: MapReduce and Distributed Filesystems
takeaways: MapReduce (Google, 2004; Hadoop as the open-source implementation on HDFS) is a programming model plus distributed execution framework: map functions emit key-value pairs, the framework partitions by key, sorts and shuffles, and reduce functions aggregate per key.
Fault tolerance comes from deterministic, side-effect-free map/reduce functions and materialized intermediate output — a crashed task is simply re-executed on another machine with the same result.

Joins in batch come in two flavors: reduce-side (sort-merge) joins shuffle both inputs so matching keys land on the same reducer — general but expensive and vulnerable to key skew; map-side joins avoid the shuffle entirely — broadcast hash join when one input fits in memory, partitioned hash join when both inputs are already partitioned the same way.

sections.heading: The Output of Batch Workflows
takeaways: Real pipelines are workflows — DAGs of jobs where one job's output becomes the next job's input — for example building search indexes, which can be document-partitioned (each partition holds a subset of documents) or term-partitioned (each partition holds the postings for a subset of terms).

MapReduce's data model is deliberately low-level — just key-value pairs with mapper/reducer callbacks — so expressing multi-stage analytics means chaining many jobs with materialized files between them.
Batch workflows maintain derived datasets (indexes, recommendation models, denormalized views) by periodically and deterministically recomputing them from the inputs.

sections.heading: Comparing Hadoop to Distributed Databases
takeaways: Hadoop is a general-purpose distributed batch platform (the book likens it to a distributed operating system for data) that tolerates raw, messy, schema-on-read data, while MPP analytic databases are specialized engines for SQL over clean, schema-on-write data.
Hadoop's core design bets: commodity hardware, fault tolerance through re-execution of deterministic tasks, and moving compute to the data (data locality) instead of dragging data to the computation.

The two approaches converged: MPP databases adopted Hadoop-era techniques such as columnar storage, and Hadoop gained fast SQL engines (Hive, Impala, Presto, Spark SQL) — so the right choice follows the workload, not the brand.

sections.heading: Beyond MapReduce
takeaways: Materialization of intermediate state is MapReduce's central tradeoff: writing every map output to the distributed filesystem before reducing gives excellent fault tolerance but pays disk I/O and replication costs at every stage; modern dataflow engines (Spark, Tez, Flink) pipeline operators or keep intermediates in memory instead.

Graph and iterative processing outgrew MapReduce: Pregel's vertex-centric bulk-synchronous-parallel model has vertices compute in parallel, exchange messages, and barrier-synchronize each superstep, with checkpoint-based fault tolerance — iterative algorithms like PageRank are wasteful on MapReduce because each iteration re-reads and re-materializes everything.

High-level APIs (Pig, Hive, Cascading, Crunch, Spark SQL/DataFrames) compile declarative queries into dataflow DAGs, letting an optimizer — not the programmer — choose join strategies and execution plans.

sections.heading: Summary
takeaways: Batch processing means bounded input, offline execution, and scheduled runs; its lineage runs from Unix pipes through MapReduce to modern dataflow engines.
The durable ideas MapReduce contributed — partitioning, sorting, and shuffle-based grouping and joins — were reused by every later engine even as the programming API changed completely.
The chapter's key design tradeoff: materializing intermediate state buys fault tolerance at the cost of performance, and each generation of engines re-negotiates that tradeoff.
